questions.question: State the four points of the particle model of matter and describe three pieces of evidence that support it.
questions.expected_answer: 1. All matter is made of tiny particles (atoms or molecules). 2. There is empty space between the particles. 3. The particles are in constant motion, moving faster at higher temperature. 4. There are forces of attraction between the particles, stronger when they are closer. Evidence: 50 mL water + 50 mL ethanol gives about 96 mL because particles fit into spaces between other particles; sugar dissolves in a full glass of water with hardly any rise in level; food colouring spreads through still water; Brownian motion — tiny particles in water or smoke particles in air jiggle randomly because they are struck by moving molecules; gases are easily compressed.

questions.question: Copy and complete a table comparing solids, liquids and gases under the headings: arrangement of particles, movement of particles, forces between particles, shape, volume and compressibility.
questions.expected_answer: Solid: closely packed in a regular pattern (lattice); vibrate about fixed positions; strong forces; fixed shape; fixed volume; not compressible. Liquid: close together but irregular; move about and slide past one another; weaker forces; no fixed shape, takes the shape of the container; fixed volume; hardly compressible. Gas: far apart (about ten particle diameters); move rapidly and randomly in straight lines, colliding; very weak forces; no fixed shape; no fixed volume, fills the container; easily compressed.

questions.question: Use the particle model to explain why a liquid can be poured but a solid cannot, why air in a syringe can be compressed but water cannot, and why the particles in a diagram of steam should be drawn the same size as those in ice.
questions.expected_answer: In a liquid the forces are weaker, so particles can slide past one another and the liquid flows; in a solid strong forces hold particles in fixed positions, so it keeps its shape. Air particles are far apart with large empty spaces, so pushing the plunger moves them closer together; water particles are already close together with very little space, so water cannot be compressed. The particles themselves do not change size or shape when the state changes; only the spaces between them and their movement change, so ice and steam particles are drawn the same size, with steam particles much further apart.
